title: Unit 2b - Pointer Arithmetic Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 2b on Pointer Arithmetic for CS 103, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 2b covering Pointer Arithmetic in CS 103. The unit explores how arithmetic operations can be performed on pointer variables, how pointer arithmetic relates to array indexing, and the concept of scaled arithmetic based on data types.
notes_text: This unit builds on prerequisite knowledge of pointer basics and data sizes. Topics covered include array names as pointers, const pointers and arguments, C string functions, pointer arithmetic with different data types, and the equivalence between pointer arithmetic and array indexing.

title: Array Names Are Pointers
summary: Array names are simply pointers to the starting address of the array. An int array name is an int*, and a char array name is a char*.
main_text: Fun Fact 3 (redux): Array names are simply pointers to the starting address of the array. Given int dat[6], dat is an int* and equivalent to &dat[0]. Given char word[6], word is a char* and equivalent to &word[0]. Example with int dat[6]: dat is of type int* and points to address 7300. The array elements dat[0] through dat[5] are stored at addresses 7300, 7304, 7308, 7312, 7316, 7320 with values 103, 170, 104, 270, 350, 360. Each element is 4 bytes apart because int is 4 bytes. Example with char word[6] = "abcde": word is of type char* and points to address 73a0. The array elements word[0] through word[5] are stored at addresses 73a0, 73a1, 73a2, 73a3, 73a4, 73a5 with values 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', '\0'. Each element is 1 byte apart because char is 1 byte.
notes_text: This is a fundamental concept: the array name decays to a pointer to the first element. This explains why arrays are passed by reference to functions -- the array name is just an address. Notice how int arrays have elements spaced 4 bytes apart while char arrays have elements spaced 1 byte apart, reflecting the size of each type.

images.description: Memory diagram showing int array dat with 6 elements at addresses 7300-7320, spaced 4 bytes apart, with pointer dat pointing to the start
Memory diagram showing char array word with 6 elements at addresses 73a0-73a5, spaced 1 byte apart, containing 'abcde' and null terminator

title: Formal Array Arguments
summary: Array arguments in function prototypes can be written as either int data[] or int* data since array names are pointers.
main_text: Because array names are pointers, array arguments in function prototypes can be written in two equivalent ways: int data[] or int* data. Example: int sum(int data[], int size) is equivalent to int sum(int* data, int size). The function body uses a for loop to iterate through the array: int total = 0; for(int i=0; i < size; i++) { total += data[i]; } return total; In main(), int vals[100] is declared. When calling sum(vals, 100), vals is passed as an int* (a pointer to the first element). The comment notes that vals is 'An int*'. The function returns the sum of all numbers in the array.
notes_text: This slide reinforces that int data[] and int* data are interchangeable in function parameter declarations. The array name vals decays to an int* when passed to the function. This is why array size information is lost when passing arrays to functions, requiring the size to be passed as a separate parameter.

images.description: Code example showing a sum function that accepts an array parameter and a main function calling it with an int array, with annotation showing vals is an int*

title: Const Pointers/Arguments Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide introducing the topic of const pointers and arguments in C/C++.
main_text: This is a section divider introducing the topic of const pointers and arguments. This section covers how the const keyword can be applied to pointer parameters to control whether a function can modify the data pointed to by the pointer.
notes_text: The const keyword is an important tool for writing safer code. By marking pointer parameters as const, you tell the compiler to enforce read-only access to the pointed-to data, catching accidental modifications at compile time.

title: Recall: Arrays Are Passed-by-Reference
summary: Arrays are passed by reference to functions, meaning the callee can change or edit the original array data, similar to shared document permissions.
main_text: When arrays are passed to functions, the function CAN CHANGE or EDIT the data in the array because arrays are passed by reference (the pointer to the original data is passed). This is analogous to shared document permissions: with a shared document you can usually set permissions to Editor (can modify) or Viewer (read-only). The question posed is whether we can do something similar with pointers and array arguments -- can we restrict a function from modifying the array data it receives?
notes_text: The shared document analogy is effective: Editor permission is like passing a non-const pointer (the function can read and write), while Viewer permission is like passing a const pointer (the function can only read). This motivates the need for the const keyword in pointer parameters.

images.description: Diagram showing array arguments flow: caller() has an Array, which is linked to an Argument that flows to callee(), illustrating that the callee accesses the same array data as the caller

title: Const or Non-Const
summary: The const modifier prevents a variable from being modified after initialization. Using const on array parameters restricts the function to read-only access.
main_text: The const modifier on a variable type means it may not be modified or changed after being initialized. Example: const int size = 5; followed by size = 6; causes a Compile Error. Why use const? Because you are your own worst enemy when programming. You make mistakes, and the more we can enlist the compiler to help catch mistakes, the better. If your intention is for a variable not to change, declare it const. A const array (or pointer) means we can GET the data (view-only) but NOT CHANGE (edit) the data. This is similar to 'Can View' vs 'Can Edit' permission on a Google doc. Non-const example: void f1(int p[], int size) allows editing with p[i] = 0 (Editor permission). Const example: void f1(const int p[], int size) allows reading with cout << p[i] but p[i] = 0 causes a compile error (Viewer permission).
notes_text: The const keyword is a compile-time safety mechanism. It does not affect runtime performance. It simply tells the compiler to flag any code that attempts to modify the const-qualified variable. This is especially valuable in large codebases where a function receiving an array pointer might accidentally modify data it should only be reading.

images.description: Three code examples: (1) const int causing compile error on reassignment, (2) non-const array parameter allowing editing marked as Editor, (3) const array parameter causing compile error on write marked as Viewer

title: Const or Non-Const Example (Exercise)
summary: Exercise asking which function parameters should be marked const. The init function modifies data so it should not be const; the sum function only reads data.
main_text: Which parameters of the functions should be marked as const? The init function: void init(_______ int data[], int size) or void init(_______ int* data, int size) reads input into data[i] using cin >> data[i], so it modifies the array. The sum function: int sum(_______ int data[], int size) or int sum(_______ int* data, int size) only reads the array with total += data[i] which is equivalent to *(data+i). Does size need to be marked const? Would it make sense to try to mark an email attachment as 'view only'? No! Since it is already a copy. Similarly, size is passed by value (it is a copy), so marking it const is unnecessary (though not harmful). In main(), int vals[100] is declared, init(vals, 100) is called to initialize, then int mysum = sum(vals, 100) computes and prints the sum.
notes_text: This exercise helps students distinguish between parameters that modify data (should not be const) and those that only read data (should be const). The email attachment analogy explains why pass-by-value parameters like size do not need const -- they are copies that cannot affect the original.

images.description: Code showing init and sum functions with blank spaces for const placement, and a main function calling both, with annotation showing vals is An int*

title: Const or Non-Const Example Solution
summary: Solution: init should NOT have const on data since it writes to the array. sum SHOULD have const on data since it only reads. size does not need const.
main_text: Solution to the const exercise. The init function: void init(int data[], int size) or void init(int* data, int size) -- NO const on data because init writes to the array via cin >> data[i]. The sum function: int sum(const int data[], int size) or int sum(const int* data, int size) -- const IS added to data because sum only reads from the array with total += data[i]. The size parameter does not need const in either function because size is passed by value (it is already a copy). Modifying the copy inside the function would not affect the caller. In main(), vals is declared as int vals[100], init(vals, 100) populates the array, and sum(vals, 100) computes the sum.
notes_text: Key takeaway: use const on pointer/array parameters when the function should only read the data, not modify it. This is a best practice that communicates intent and catches bugs at compile time. Pass-by-value parameters like int size are inherently safe copies, so const is optional on them.

images.description: Code showing the solved version with const added to sum's data parameter but not to init's data parameter, with annotation showing vals is An int*

title: C (not C++) String Function/Library (#include <cstring>)
summary: Overview of the C string library functions including strlen, strcmp, strcpy, strcat, and strchr, accessed via #include <cstring> in C++ or <string.h> in C.
main_text: A library of functions was provided to perform operations on character arrays representing strings. In C++, include <cstring>; in C, include <string.h>. Key functions: int strlen(const char *dest) or int strlen(const char dest[]) -- returns the length of the string. int strcmp(const char *str1, const char *str2) -- returns 0 if equal, >0 if first non-equal char in str1 is alphanumerically larger, <0 otherwise. char *strcpy(char *dest, const char *src) -- copies src string into dest. char *strcat(char *dest, const char *src) -- concatenates src to the end of dest. char *strchr(const char *str, char c) -- finds first occurrence of character c in str, returning a pointer to that character or NULL if the character is not found. Notice how const is used: source/read-only parameters use const char*, while destination/writable parameters use char* without const.
notes_text: These C string functions predate C++ std::string and work directly with char arrays. Notice the consistent use of const: parameters that are only read are marked const (like src in strcpy), while parameters that will be modified are not (like dest in strcpy). This demonstrates real-world application of const correctness covered in the previous slides.

title: Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing pointer arithmetic and arrays, with prerequisites of pointer basics and data sizes.
main_text: This is a section divider introducing the topic of Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays. Prerequisites for this section are Pointer Basics and Data Sizes. This section will cover how arithmetic operations on pointers work, how they relate to array indexing, and the concept of scaled arithmetic based on the pointed-to type's size.
notes_text: Students should be comfortable with pointer declaration, dereferencing, address-of operator, and the sizes of fundamental data types (int = 4 bytes, double = 8 bytes, char = 1 byte) before proceeding.

title: Review Questions on Data Sizes and Arrays
summary: Review questions covering int size (4 bytes), double size (8 bytes), contiguous array storage, and calculating array element addresses.
main_text: Review questions to recall prerequisite knowledge. The size of an int is how many bytes? (Answer: 4). The size of a double is how many bytes? (Answer: 8). True/False: The elements of an array are stored contiguously (i.e., next to each other) in memory. (Answer: True). In an array of integers, if dat[0] lived at address 0x200, dat[1] would live at...? Since each int is 4 bytes and elements are contiguous, dat[1] would be at 0x204 (0x200 + 4).
notes_text: These review questions establish the foundation for understanding pointer arithmetic. Knowing that int is 4 bytes and double is 8 bytes is critical because pointer arithmetic scales by the size of the type. Contiguous storage means we can navigate arrays by stepping through memory addresses.

title: What Changes? Dereferencing and Incrementing
summary: Demonstrates the difference between modifying the value at the pointer (*ptr += 1) versus modifying the pointer itself. Dereferencing then incrementing changes the pointed-to data.
main_text: What effect does the highlighted line of code have? Given char word[6] = "abcde" and char* ptr = &word[2], ptr holds address 73a2 which points to 'c'. The expression (*ptr) += 1 or (*ptr)++ goes to address 73a2 and adds 1 to the value stored there. Since 'c' has ASCII value 99, adding 1 gives 100 which is 'd'. So this changes 'c' to 'd' at word[2]. The key insight is that parentheses around *ptr mean we first dereference the pointer to get the value, then increment that value. The pointer itself does not change -- it still points to address 73a2.
notes_text: This slide sets up the critical distinction between (*ptr)++ which modifies the data at the address, and ptr++ which modifies the address stored in the pointer. The parentheses are essential: (*ptr)++ dereferences first then increments the value, while *ptr++ would increment the pointer first due to operator precedence.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char array word at addresses 73a0-73a5 with values 'a' through 'e' and null terminator. Pointer ptr holds 73a2. After (*ptr)+=1, the value at 73a2 changes from 'c' to 'd'.

title: So, What Are We Changing Here? (Exercise)
summary: Contrasts (*ptr) += 1 which changes the value at the address, with ptr += 1 which changes the address stored in the pointer itself.
main_text: This slide contrasts two operations side by side. On the left: char word[6] = "abcde"; char* ptr = &word[2]; (*ptr) += 1 or (*ptr)++ -- this modifies the value at the address (changes what the pointer points to). On the right: char word[6] = "abcde"; char* ptr = &word[2]; ptr += 1 or ptr++ -- what is being updated here? The question asks students to identify that in the right-hand code, it is the pointer variable itself (the address it stores) that is being updated, not the data it points to.
notes_text: The visual contrast between left and right code blocks makes the distinction clear. On the left, the asterisk dereferences first so the value changes. On the right, there is no dereference, so the address in ptr changes. This is a common source of confusion for students learning pointers.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison of two code blocks with an arrow between them. Left shows (*ptr)+=1 modifying the value, right shows ptr+=1 modifying the pointer. Below is a memory diagram of the char array.

title: So, What Are We Changing Here? (Solution)
summary: Solution: ptr += 1 updates the address stored in the pointer from 73a2 to 73a3, making it point to the next element. This is pointer arithmetic.
main_text: The address stored in the pointer is updated. Given char word[6] = "abcde" and char* ptr = &word[2], ptr initially holds 73a2. After ptr += 1 or ptr++, the pointer now holds 73a3 (was 73a2, crossed out to show 73a3). Adding 1 to the address in ptr changes what the pointer points at -- it now points to word[3] ('d') instead of word[2] ('c'). The data in the array is unchanged. The key takeaway is: we can perform arithmetic on pointers to change what they point at. This is the foundation of pointer arithmetic.
notes_text: This is the pivotal slide that introduces the concept of pointer arithmetic. The pointer is a variable holding an address, and we can add or subtract from that address just like any other number. For char*, adding 1 moves to the next byte since sizeof(char) = 1.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char* ptr with value 73a2 crossed out and replaced with 73a3, with an arrow moving from word[2] to word[3] in the char array at addresses 73a0-73a5

title: A Logical Progression to Pointer Arithmetic
summary: Logical reasoning: pointers store addresses, addresses are numbers, arithmetic works on numbers, therefore arithmetic can be performed on pointers.
main_text: A logical progression leads to the concept of pointer arithmetic. Consider: Pointers are variables storing addresses. Addresses are just numbers. We can perform arithmetic on numbers. Therefore, we should be able to perform arithmetic on pointers! Conclusion: We can perform addition or subtraction on pointer variables (i.e., addresses) just like any other variable. This is known as pointer arithmetic.
notes_text: This slide formalizes the intuition built in the previous slides. Pointer arithmetic is not a special operation -- it follows naturally from the fact that addresses are numeric values stored in variables. The compiler handles the type-aware scaling automatically, which is covered in subsequent slides.

title: Pointer Arithmetic Examples with char*
summary: Demonstrates pointer arithmetic with char* on a character array. Adding 3 then subtracting 2 from a char pointer moves it through byte-sized elements.
main_text: Examples of pointer arithmetic with char pointers. Given char word[6] = "abcde" and char* ptr = &word[1], ptr initially holds address 73a1. After ptr = ptr + 3 (or ptr += 3), ptr now holds 73a4, pointing to word[4] ('e'). After ptr -= 2, ptr now holds 73a2, pointing to word[2] ('c'). For char*, each increment of 1 moves the pointer by 1 byte since sizeof(char) = 1. We can perform arithmetic on pointers to change what they point at.
notes_text: With char pointers, the arithmetic is straightforward because sizeof(char) is 1 byte. Adding n to a char* moves the pointer by exactly n bytes in memory. This direct byte-level correspondence will contrast with int* and double* in upcoming slides where the scaling factor differs.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char* ptr starting at 73a1, then moving to 73a4 after ptr+=3, then to 73a2 after ptr-=2. Arrows connect the pointer to the corresponding positions in the word array at addresses 73a0-73a5.

title: Step Size Analogy with House Addresses
summary: Mailperson analogy: moving to the next house (+1 house) requires incrementing the address by +2 because even and odd addresses are on opposite sides of the street.
main_text: A mailperson delivers mail to each house by going from one house (house x) to the next (house x+1). But what address is house x+1? Usually, even addresses are on one side of the street while odd are on the other. If one house is 2800 Catalina Ave, then moving to the NEXT address/house (i.e., moving +1 house away) actually requires incrementing the address by +2. So +1 house equals +2 addresses. This analogy illustrates that the step size to move to the next item depends on how items are organized -- the logical step (next house) is different from the physical step (address increment).
notes_text: This real-world analogy directly maps to pointer arithmetic: the logical step (next array element) may require a different physical step (number of bytes) depending on the data type size. For int* (+1 element = +4 bytes), for double* (+1 element = +8 bytes), for char* (+1 element = +1 byte). The compiler handles this translation automatically.

images.description: Photo of a mail carrier delivering mail, alongside a diagram of house addresses showing even numbers (2800, 2802, 2804, 2806) on one side and odd numbers (2801, 2803, 2805, 2807) on the other, with annotation showing +1 house = +2 addresses

title: The Impact of Types on Pointer Arithmetic (Question)
summary: Asks what address an int* pointer would update to after ptr += 1, and whether simply adding 1 to the raw address (7305) would be desirable.
main_text: What address would ptr update to? Would that be desirable? Given int dat[6] = { ... } with elements at addresses 7300, 7304, 7308, 7312, 7316, 7320 and int* ptr = &data[1], ptr holds address 7304. If ptr += 1 naively added 1 to the address, ptr would become 7305. But would 7305 be a valid location? The question mark (7305??) suggests this is problematic. No integer starts at address 7305 -- it falls in the middle of dat[1] (which occupies bytes 7304-7307).
notes_text: This slide builds tension by showing that naive byte-level addition would land in the middle of an int, which is meaningless. This motivates the need for scaled/type-aware pointer arithmetic that the compiler provides automatically.

images.description: Memory diagram showing int array dat with 6 elements at addresses 7300-7320. int* ptr points to 7304 (dat[1]). The question 7305?? is highlighted next to ptr += 1 to show this would land in the middle of an integer.

title: The Impact of Types on Pointer Arithmetic (Answer)
summary: Incrementing an int* by 1 byte is useless since no integer starts there. Moving 1 integer requires stepping 4 bytes because integers are 4 bytes each.
main_text: Incrementing an int* by just 1 does not help. No integer starts at 7305! We likely meant 'Move 1 INTEGER (or INTEGER-sized step) over.' Because integers are 4 bytes each, to move 1 integer away, we have to take steps of 4 addresses at a time. Given int dat[6] with int* ptr = &data[2] at address 7308 (note: originally at 7304 but diagram shows 7304 crossed out), after ptr += 1 the pointer should move to 7308, not 7305. The address 7305 is shown with a prohibition symbol to indicate it is an invalid/undesirable target.
notes_text: This slide resolves the problem posed on the previous slide. The compiler knows the type of the pointer and automatically multiplies the offset by sizeof(type). For int* (4 bytes), ptr += 1 actually adds 4 to the raw address. This ensures the pointer always lands on a valid data boundary.

images.description: Memory diagram showing int array dat at addresses 7300-7320. int* ptr at 7304 with 7305 marked with a prohibition symbol. Arrow shows ptr moving from 7304 to 7308 (skipping over 4 bytes) after ptr += 1.

title: Key Idea: Scaled Arithmetic
summary: The number added/subtracted to a pointer is implicitly SCALED (multiplied) by the size of the type pointed to. For int*, +1 adds 4; for double*, +1 adds 8.
main_text: Thankfully, the number added/subtracted is implicitly SCALED (multiplied) by the size of the type pointed to. For an int*, adding 1 actually adds 1*4 (since sizeof(int) = 4). For a double*, adding 1 actually adds 1*8 (since sizeof(double) = 8). This means pointer arithmetic always moves the pointer by whole data-element steps, ensuring it lands on valid data boundaries. The compiler handles this scaling automatically based on the pointer's declared type.
notes_text: This is the central concept of the unit. Scaled arithmetic is what makes pointer arithmetic practical and safe. Without it, programmers would have to manually multiply offsets by type sizes. The formula is: new_address = old_address + n * sizeof(type). This applies to both addition and subtraction.

title: Integer Pointer Arithmetic (Exercise)
summary: Exercise for int* pointer arithmetic: starting at address 7304, compute the result of ptr += 3 and then ptr -= 2, using implicit scaling by sizeof(int).
main_text: For pointer arithmetic, the number added/subtracted is implicitly scaled (multiplied) by the size of the type pointed to, ensuring the resulting address points to a valid data item. Given int dat[6] with elements at addresses 7300-7320 and int* ptr = &dat[1] at address 7304. Exercise: ptr += 3 means 7304 + ___ * sizeof(int), which equals 73__. ptr -= 2 means ____ - ___ * sizeof(int), which equals 73__. The blanks are left for students to fill in. The int array has values 103, 170, 104, 270, 350, 360 at addresses 7300, 7304, 7308, 7312, 7316, 7320.
notes_text: Students should compute: ptr += 3 gives 7304 + 3*4 = 7304 + 12 = 7316 (pointing to dat[4]). Then ptr -= 2 gives 7316 - 2*4 = 7316 - 8 = 7308 (pointing to dat[2]). This exercise reinforces that for int*, each logical step of 1 translates to a physical step of 4 bytes.

images.description: Diagram showing int* ptr at address 7304 with blank computation boxes for ptr+=3 and ptr-=2. Memory array dat shown at bottom with addresses 7300-7320 and values 103-360.

title: Integer Pointer Arithmetic (Solution)
summary: Solution: ptr += 3 gives 7304 + 3*4 = 7316 (dat[4]). ptr -= 2 gives 7316 - 2*4 = 7308 (dat[2]). Each step scales by sizeof(int) = 4.
main_text: Solution to the integer pointer arithmetic exercise. For pointer arithmetic, the number added/subtracted is implicitly scaled (multiplied) by the size of the type pointed to, ensuring the resulting address points to a valid data item. Given int* ptr = &dat[1] at address 7304: ptr += 3 means 7304 + 3*4 = 7316. The pointer now points to dat[4] (value 350). ptr -= 2 means 7316 - 2*4 = 7308. The pointer now points to dat[2] (value 104). Arrows in the diagram show the pointer moving from 7304 to 7316 after the addition, then from 7316 to 7308 after the subtraction.
notes_text: The computation is straightforward: multiply the offset by sizeof(int) = 4. ptr += 3 moves forward 3 integers (12 bytes), ptr -= 2 moves backward 2 integers (8 bytes). The final position dat[2] can be verified: starting at dat[1], +3 gives dat[4], then -2 gives dat[2].

images.description: Diagram showing int* ptr computation: 7304 + 3*4 = 7316, then 7316 - 2*4 = 7308. Arrows point from the computed addresses to the corresponding positions in the int array dat at addresses 7300-7320.

title: Double Pointer Arithmetic (Exercise)
summary: Exercise for double* pointer arithmetic: starting at address 7308, compute ptr += 3 and ptr -= 4 using implicit scaling by sizeof(double) = 8.
main_text: For pointer arithmetic, the number added/subtracted is implicitly scaled (multiplied) by the size of the type pointed to, ensuring the resulting address points to a valid data item. Given double gpa[6] with values 3.5, 2.9, 3.7, 3.9, 2.6, 3.2 at addresses 7300, 7308, 7316, 7324, 7332, 7340 (each double is 8 bytes apart). double *ptr = &gpa[1] at address 7308. Exercise: ptr += 3 means 7308 + ___ * sizeof(double), result is 73__. ptr -= 4 means ____ - ___ * sizeof(double), result is 73__. Students must fill in the blanks using sizeof(double) = 8.
notes_text: Students should compute: ptr += 3 gives 7308 + 3*8 = 7308 + 24 = 7332 (pointing to gpa[4]). Then ptr -= 4 gives 7332 - 4*8 = 7332 - 32 = 7300 (pointing to gpa[0]). Note the double array has elements spaced 8 bytes apart, twice the spacing of int arrays.

images.description: Diagram showing double* ptr at address 7308 with blank computation boxes for ptr+=3 and ptr-=4. Double array gpa shown at bottom with addresses 7300-7340 spaced 8 bytes apart, with values 3.5, 2.9, 3.7, 3.9, 2.6, 3.2.

title: Double Pointer Arithmetic (Solution)
summary: Solution: ptr += 3 gives 7308 + 3*8 = 7332 (gpa[4]). ptr -= 4 gives 7332 - 4*8 = 7300 (gpa[0]). Each step scales by sizeof(double) = 8.
main_text: Solution to the double pointer arithmetic exercise. Given double *ptr = &gpa[1] at address 7308: ptr += 3 means 7308 + 3*8 = 7332. The pointer now points to gpa[4] (value 2.6). ptr -= 4 means 7332 - 4*8 = 7300. The pointer now points to gpa[0] (value 3.5). The double array gpa has 6 elements at addresses 7300, 7308, 7316, 7324, 7332, 7340 with values 3.5, 2.9, 3.7, 3.9, 2.6, 3.2. Arrows show the pointer moving from 7308 to 7332 then to 7300.
notes_text: Comparing with the int* exercise: for int*, the scale factor is 4; for double*, it is 8. The compiler determines the scale factor from the pointer type. This is why the type of a pointer matters -- it controls how arithmetic operations translate to byte offsets in memory.

images.description: Diagram showing double* ptr computation: 7308 + 3*8 = 7332, then 7332 - 4*8 = 7300. Arrows point from computed addresses to positions in the double array gpa at addresses 7300-7340.

title: Arrays vs Pointers: Equivalent Access Methods
summary: Common array syntax (dat[i] = 0) and walking pointer syntax (*ptr1 = 0; ptr1++) produce the same behavior -- both set all array elements to 0.
main_text: Both methods below result in the same behavior -- they set all elements of the array to 0. The array dat has 6 elements at addresses 73a0-73b4 with values 103, 170, 104, 270, 350, 360. An int* ptr1 is initialized to 73a0 (the start of the array). Common Array Syntax: int main() { int dat[5]; for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { dat[i] = 0; } }. Walking Pointer approach: int main() { int dat[5]; int *ptr1 = dat; for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { *ptr1 = 0; ptr1++; } }. In the walking pointer approach, *ptr1 = 0 sets the current element to 0, then ptr1++ advances the pointer to the next integer (adding 4 bytes due to scaled arithmetic).
notes_text: The 'walking pointer' technique is a common pattern in C/C++ programming. Instead of using array indexing with dat[i], you maintain a pointer that walks through the array element by element. Each ptr1++ moves to the next element. Both approaches compile to essentially the same machine code. Note: the loop bound of 10 with array size 5 would cause a buffer overflow bug in practice.

images.description: Memory diagram showing int* ptr1 at 73a0 pointing to the start of int array dat. Below are two side-by-side code blocks: Common Array Syntax using dat[i]=0 and Walking Pointer using *ptr1=0 with ptr1++.

title: A Quick Tangent: Array Element Addresses
summary: The address of the i-th element in an array is computed as start_addr + i * sizeof_type, analogous to finding the position of the i-th train car.
main_text: Consider a train with many copies of the same car. The 0th car starts at point A on the number line. Each car is 5 meters long. Write an arithmetic expression for where the i-th car is located: A + i*5. Suppose an array of integers starts at memory address A. Write an expression for where the i-th integer starts: A + i*4 (since sizeof(int) = 4). Suppose an array of doubles starts at memory address A. Write an expression for where the i-th double starts: A + i*8 (since sizeof(double) = 8). The general formula for the address of the i-th element is: start_addr + i * sizeof_type.
notes_text: The train car analogy makes the address formula intuitive. Just as you find the i-th train car by multiplying the car length by i and adding to the starting position, you find the i-th array element by multiplying the element size by i and adding to the base address. This is exactly what the compiler does with array indexing: data[i] is translated to *(data + i), which uses the formula start_addr + i * sizeof_type.

images.description: Diagram of three train cars labeled 0th car, 1st car, 2nd car on a number line at positions A, A+5, A+10, illustrating how the i-th item's position is calculated by multiplying index by item size

title: Pointer Arithmetic and Array Indexing Equivalence
summary: Pointer arithmetic and array indexing are the same operation: *(data + i) is equivalent to data[i]. The brackets imply dereferencing with scaled offset.
main_text: Pointer arithmetic and array indexing are really the same! Pointer syntax vs. Array syntax: *(data + i) <=> data[i]. Breaking this down: data is the start address, + i implicitly scales by i*sizeof_type, and * (dereference) operator gets the value at that address. The array brackets [] imply dereference (*). So (data + i) computes the address of the i-th value in an array, and * (the dereference operator) gets its value. Example: int array data with values 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 at addresses 7300, 7304, 7308, 7312, 7316, 7320. data+0 = 7300, data+1 = 7304, data+2 = 7308, data+3 = 7312, data+4 = 7316, data+5 = 7320.
notes_text: This is one of the most important equivalences in C/C++. The bracket operator [] is syntactic sugar for pointer arithmetic plus dereference. Understanding this equivalence explains many behaviors: why arrays are zero-indexed (the first element is at offset 0), why array bounds are not checked (pointer arithmetic has no bounds checking), and why arrays and pointers are interchangeable in many contexts.

images.description: Annotated equation showing *(data + i) <=> data[i], with labels identifying data as Start Address and i as implicitly scaled by i*sizeof_type. Below is a memory diagram of int array with values 10-15 showing data+0 through data+5 labels above the addresses.

title: Big Idea: Array Names and Pointers are Interchangeable
summary: Once an array is allocated, its name is a pointer and a pointer can be used as an array name. data[i] is computed as *(data + i) by the computer.
main_text: Big idea: Array names and pointers are interchangeable. Once an array is allocated, an array name is a pointer and a pointer can be used as an array name! Array names are pointers: given the declaration int dat[10], dat is an int* (const int*). Given the declaration char str[6], str is a char* (const char*). When we write [] like dat[i], the computer performs *(dat + i). Examples: int dat[5] = {10,11,12,13,14}; *dat = 1; is the same as dat[0] = 1. int *p = dat; p[1] = p[2]-8; uses the pointer as an array name, same as dat[1] = dat[2] - 8. The diagram shows int* p holding address 7300, same as dat (Const int*), both pointing to the array starting at 7300.
notes_text: A subtle but important distinction: while array names and pointers can be used interchangeably for accessing elements, array names are const pointers -- you cannot reassign an array name to point somewhere else (dat = other_array is illegal). A pointer variable, however, can be reassigned. Also note that array names know their size at compile time (in the declaring scope), while pointers do not carry size information.

images.description: Memory diagram showing int* p at address 7300 and dat as Const int* also at 7300, both pointing to the start of int array with values 10-14 at addresses 7300-7316

title: Array Names and Pointers Exercise
summary: Tracing exercise: given int dat[6] and int* ptr = &dat[2], shows how ptr[0] = 5 sets dat[2] to 5 and ptr[2] = 42 sets dat[4] to 42.
main_text: Can you trace through and understand this code. Given int dat[6] with elements at addresses 73a0, 73a4, 73a8, 73ac, 73b0, 73b4 (using hex addresses) with values 103, 170, 104, 270, 350, 360. int* ptr = &dat[2] means ptr holds address 73a8. ptr[0] = 5 sets the value at ptr's address (73a8, which is dat[2]) to 5. ptr[2] = 42 sets the value at ptr+2 (73a8 + 2*4 = 73b0, which is dat[4]) to 42. The diagram shows dat with pointer arithmetic labels (dat+1, dat+2, etc. with hex addresses 73a0+1*4, 73a0+2*4, etc.) and ptr with its own relative offsets (ptr-2, ptr-1, ptr, ptr+1, ptr+2, ptr+3 at addresses 73a8-2*4, 73a8-1*4, 73a8, 73a8+1*4, 73a8+2*4, 73a8+3*4).
notes_text: This exercise demonstrates that a pointer into the middle of an array creates a new 'view' of the array. ptr[0] refers to dat[2], ptr[1] refers to dat[3], etc. Negative indices are also valid: ptr[-1] would be dat[1] and ptr[-2] would be dat[0]. This is a powerful but dangerous feature -- there is no bounds checking.

images.description: Memory diagram showing int array dat with both dat-relative labels (dat, dat+1, ..., dat+5) and ptr-relative labels (ptr-2, ptr-1, ptr, ptr+1, ptr+2, ptr+3) with hex address calculations shown for each

title: Arrays vs Pointers: Three Equivalent Methods
summary: Three methods to initialize an array produce the same result: array indexing (ptr1[i]=0), explicit pointer arithmetic (*(ptr2+i)=0), and walking pointer (*ptr3=0; ptr3++).
main_text: All 3 methods below perform the same task of initializing the array. Which do you prefer? Remember, your goal is to make your code readable (option 1) but you should understand all 3. The array dat has 6 elements at addresses 73a0-73b4 with values 103, 170, 104, 270, 350, 360. int* ptr1/2/3 all start at 73a0. Common Array Syntax: int *ptr1 = dat; for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { ptr1[i] = 0; } -- equivalent to dat[i] = 0. Explicit pointer arithmetic: int *ptr2 = dat; for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { *(ptr2+i) = 0; } -- uses dereference of pointer plus offset. Walking Pointer: int *ptr3 = dat; for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { *ptr3 = 0; ptr3++; } -- dereferences current position then advances.
notes_text: Option 1 (array syntax with pointer) is most readable and preferred for production code. Option 2 (explicit pointer arithmetic) makes the underlying mechanism visible. Option 3 (walking pointer) is efficient for sequential access but harder to read. All three compile to nearly identical machine code. Understanding all three is important for reading C/C++ code written by others.

images.description: Memory diagram at top showing int array dat, followed by three side-by-side code blocks showing Common Array Syntax, Explicit pointer arithmetic, and Walking Pointer methods for initializing the array

title: Pointer Arithmetic Examples (Exercise)
summary: Complex exercise tracing pointer arithmetic with int and double arrays, including *ptr1=104, ptr1=ptr1+2, (*ptr1)++, ptr1--, and double pointer operations.
main_text: The number added/subtracted to the pointer is implicitly scaled (multiplied) by the size of the type pointed to, ensuring the resulting address points to a valid data item. Memory layout shows: dat at 73a0 with values {103, 5, 1}, int len=0 at 73ac, double gpa[3] = {3.7, 3.5, 3.1} starting at 73b0. Code to trace: int *ptr1 = dat; sets ptr1 to 73a0. *ptr1 = 104; sets dat[0] to 104. ptr1 = ptr1 + 2; address increments by 2*sizeof(int) = 2*4 = 8, so ptr1 moves from 73a0 to 73a8, pointing to dat[2]. (*ptr1)++; increments the value at dat[2]. ptr1--; address decrements by 1*sizeof(int) = 4, ptr1 moves to 73a4. double *ptr2 = gpa; sets ptr2 to 73b0. ptr2 += 2; address increments by 2*sizeof(double) = 2*8 = 16, ptr2 moves to 73c0. *ptr2++ = 4.0; sets the dereferenced value to 4.0 then increments ptr2 address by 1*sizeof(double) = 8. Final question: *ptr2 = 2.9; What if?
notes_text: This comprehensive exercise combines multiple pointer operations. Key points: *ptr1 = 104 modifies the value, ptr1 + 2 moves by 2 ints (8 bytes), (*ptr1)++ modifies the value then is equivalent to the value plus 1, ptr1-- moves back 1 int (4 bytes). For the double pointer, ptr2 += 2 moves by 16 bytes. The *ptr2++ = 4.0 expression uses post-increment: it sets the current location to 4.0 first, then advances ptr2. The final *ptr2 = 2.9 question asks students to consider what ptr2 now points to after the post-increment.

images.description: Detailed memory map showing addresses 73a0-73d4 with int array dat, int len, double array gpa, int* ptr1, and double* ptr2 variables with their values and pointer arrows. Blanks left for students to fill in computed addresses.

title: Pointer Arithmetic Examples (Solution)
summary: Solution showing traced memory state: dat becomes {104,5,2}, ptr1 ends at 73a8 then 73a4, gpa[2] becomes 4.0, ptr2 ends at 73c8 after post-increment.
main_text: Solution to the pointer arithmetic tracing exercise. Starting state: dat = {103, 5, 1}, len = 0, gpa = {3.7, 3.5, 3.1}. int *ptr1 = dat; ptr1 = 73a0. *ptr1 = 104; dat[0] changes from 103 to 104. ptr1 = ptr1 + 2; addr increments by 2*4 (2*sizeof(int)) = 8, ptr1 = 73a0 + 8 = 73a8. (*ptr1)++; value at 73a8 (dat[2]) changes from 1 to 2. ptr1--; addr decrements by 1*4 (1*sizeof(int)) = 4, ptr1 = 73a8 - 4 = 73a4. double *ptr2 = gpa; ptr2 = 73b0. ptr2 += 2; ptr2 addr + 2*8 (2*sizeof(double)) = 16, ptr2 = 73b0 + 16 = 73c0. *ptr2++ = 4.0; sets value at 73c0 (gpa[2]) from 3.1 to 4.0, then increments ptr2 addr by 1*8 (1*sizeof(double)) = 8, ptr2 = 73c0 + 8 = 73c8. The memory diagram shows updated values with old values crossed out. Final state: ptr1 at 73a4, ptr2 at 73c8 (which points to the int* ptr1 storage area). *ptr2 = 2.9 would overwrite ptr1's stored address, which would be a type-aliasing bug.
notes_text: The final question *ptr2 = 2.9 is a trap: ptr2 (a double*) has been incremented past the gpa array and now points to the memory where ptr1 is stored (73c8). Writing a double value there would corrupt ptr1's address -- a dangerous out-of-bounds write demonstrating why pointer arithmetic must be used carefully within array bounds.

images.description: Detailed memory map showing final state after all operations. Old values crossed out and new values written: dat[0]=104, dat[2]=2, gpa[2]=4.0. ptr1 at 73a4, ptr2 at 73c8. Arrows show pointer positions.

title: Pointer Arithmetic with int* and double* (Backup Reference)
summary: Reference slide showing scaled pointer arithmetic for int* (scale by 4) and double* (scale by 8), with memory diagrams for both types.
main_text: Pointer arithmetic implicitly scales the added value based on the type of pointer. For an int*, adding +2 really adds +2 * sizeof(int) = +2*4 = 8 so that the pointer will point 2 integers away. For a double*, adding +2 really adds +2 * sizeof(double) = +2*8 = 16 so that the pointer will point 2 doubles away. Double example: double gpa[6] with values 3.5, 2.9, 3.7, 3.9, 2.6, 3.2 at addresses 73a0, 73a8, 73b0, 73b8, 73c0, 73c8 (spaced 8 bytes apart). double* p2 = gpa+2 sets p2 to 73b0. p2 += <offset> would move by offset * 8 bytes. Relative positions: p2-2 at 73b0-2*8, p2-1 at 73b0-1*8, p2 at 73b0, p2+1 at 73b0+1*8, p2+2 at 73b0+2*8, p2+3 at 73b0+3*8.
notes_text: This backup slide reinforces the scaling concept with concrete memory layouts for both int* and double*. The key formula remains: new_address = current_address + n * sizeof(pointed_to_type). For int* the scale factor is 4 bytes, for double* it is 8 bytes.

images.description: Memory diagram showing double array gpa with 6 elements at addresses 73a0-73c8 spaced 8 bytes apart. double* p2 at 73b0 (gpa+2) with relative offset labels p2-2 through p2+3 and their hex address calculations.

title: Pointer Arithmetic with char* (Backup Reference)
summary: Reference slide showing scaled pointer arithmetic for char* where the scale factor is 1 (sizeof(char) = 1), so address changes match the offset directly.
main_text: Pointer arithmetic implicitly scales the added value based on the type of pointer. For a char*, adding +2 really adds +2 * sizeof(char) = +2*1 = 2 so that the pointer will point 2 chars away. Example: char ltr[6] with values 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f' at addresses 73a0, 73a1, 73a2, 73a3, 73a4, 73a5 (spaced 1 byte apart). char* p3 = ltr+2 sets p3 to 73a2. p3 += <offset> would move by offset * 1 bytes. Relative positions: p3-2 at 73a2-2*1, p3-1 at 73a2-1*1, p3 at 73a2, p3+1 at 73a2+1*1, p3+2 at 73a2+2*1, p3+3 at 73a2+3*1. For char*, the scaling factor is 1, so the logical offset equals the physical byte offset.
notes_text: Char pointers are the simplest case of pointer arithmetic because sizeof(char) = 1. The address offset directly equals the logical element offset. This is why char* (or unsigned char*) is often used for raw byte-level memory manipulation. Comparing all three types: char* scales by 1, int* scales by 4, double* scales by 8.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char array ltr with 6 elements at addresses 73a0-73a5 spaced 1 byte apart. char* p3 at 73a2 (ltr+2) with relative offset labels p3-2 through p3+3 and their hex address calculations showing multiplication by 1.
